newsitem.title: USA: Congress fails to get disaster aid bill compromise.
newsitem.headline: Congress fails to get disaster aid bill compromise.

text.p: House and Senate negotiators were unable to reach a compromise on a $8.4 billion disaster aid bill Wednesday due to disputes over government spending, Alaska road building and other issues.

The legislation contains $5.5 billion to aid more than 30 states hit by floods, mudslides and harsh weather. It provides about $2 billion for U.S. peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and continued U.S. military flights in the Gulf.
Lawmakers were in broad agreement on the disaster aid. The problem was that the must-pass spending bill became a magnet for a host of unrelated items.

After days of inconclusive talks, House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston threatened to pull the plug and put what had been an "emergency" measure on hold until early June when Congress returns from a week-long recess.

The Louisiana Republican also suggested he might try to pull some key provisions out of the legislation and try to pass them as a separate bill, free of the special interest baggage that threatens to sink the entire package.

"I think we have reached a limit here beyond which we are not prepared to travel," Livingston told an evening meeting in which negotiators made little progress. The negotiators may meet again Thursday.
He told reporters the measure was at such a "late stage I would not be surprised if the bill would have to await further action following the break."
President Clinton has threatened to veto the measure unless lawmakers back off from several key provisions.

One big hurdle is a Republican provision to automatically keep the government running next year if Congress and the White House could not agree on spending bills. Clinton has threatened to veto the entire bill over that proposal.

White House officials argue the plan would provide $18 billion less for domestic spending than Republicans agreed to as part of a new balanced budget deal. They also say it would take the pressure off Congress to compromise on spending bills.

Republican leaders are eager to avoid a repeat of two unpopular government shutdowns during fiscal 1996, which voters blamed on their party. They profess amazement that Clinton would be willing to risk another shutdown.
"Right now it's in the bill, it will stay in the bill," said Texas Republican Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison.
The White House is adamantly opposed to a proposal by Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Ted Stevens making it easier to build roads on federal lands in Alaska.

The administration said the Alaska Republican's plan could allow roads in pristine areas all over the state. Stevens argues Alaska and other western areas need a better transportation system to spur economic development.

Another big dispute is a Senate plan barring the government from spending money on sampling or other statistical techniques for the 2000 census. Sampling could provide a more accurate count of minorities.

Lawmakers did agree to the full $76 million the White House wanted for nutrition aid for poor women and children. They retained Massachusetts-based Crane and Co.'s contract to supply paper for U.S. currency and allowed importation of some polar bear skins.
